passage:
Dear Noor,

You asked how the product is going, and I owe you an honest answer. Every time the sales head raised his voice in a review, I changed the plan. When the operations head pushed just as hard the next week, I changed it back. The support and design teams said little, so I assumed they were fine. Last Friday two of the designers told me they've stopped bringing ideas because nothing they say ever sticks. The app has three priorities now and nobody can say what it is for. I kept telling myself I was keeping the peace, but really I was avoiding the discomfort of saying no. I'm going to write the goal on one page and check every request against it.

Anirban

qa.q: What did the two designers tell Anirban last Friday?
qa.a: They said they've stopped bringing ideas because nothing they say ever sticks.

qa.q: What does Anirban seem to feel about the changes of plan, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anirban sounds regretful: the letter admits that keeping the peace was really avoiding the discomfort of saying no.

qa.q: What other approach could Anirban use in reviews, and why?
qa.a: Anirban could ask each team to state its need in turn and test each request against the one-page goal, so decisions follow the goal instead of the loudest voice.

qa.q: How do the designers experience these reviews?
qa.a: They feel ignored, since ideas never stick when louder voices decide, so they stopped offering them.

grounding: Shows a manager giving in to the most forceful executive each time, leaving quieter teams ignored and the product without a clear direction.

passage: Shalini, you asked why the product I manage feels like a mess. I can tell you exactly. It's me. I'm Uma, and for a year I gave in to whoever shouted loudest. The sales director would storm into my cabin, and I'd move his feature to the top. Then the CEO's office would call, and I'd move theirs. The support team kept sending polite emails about customers who couldn't reset passwords. Polite emails don't storm into cabins. So they waited. Eight months. Last week the support lead resigned. Her exit note said, 'We were never heard.' And when I look at the product now, it's twelve half-finished features for three loud people, and a password reset that still doesn't work. Nobody would call that a direction.

qa.q: How long did the support team's password issue wait?
How does Uma feel about the support lead's exit note?
qa.a: Uma feels guilty and ashamed, seeing that the quieter team was never heard.

qa.q: What approach could Uma use instead to set priorities?
qa.a: Uma could agree criteria like customer impact with all teams and score requests openly, so the loudest voice doesn't decide.

qa.q: How did the support team experience the year?
qa.a: They felt ignored while customers struggled with password resets, so much that their lead resigned.

grounding: It shows a manager giving in to the most forceful executives, leaving quieter teams ignored and the product drifting without a direction.

passage: I'm Farida, and I've been on Sahil's team for two years. He's kind, and he hates conflict. I noticed it most in planning meetings. When Mr Bhatia from sales raised his voice, his request went on the board in red. When our design lead, who speaks softly, said the checkout was confusing customers, Sahil nodded and wrote it at the bottom. In March the finance head sent an angry email; the next day her report jumped the queue. By June we had shipped three features for sales, two for finance, and nothing the designers or the call centre had asked for. The call centre stopped attending planning. Checkout complaints doubled. Sahil looked exhausted in every meeting. I don't know what he was thinking, but the product no longer seemed to be going anywhere.

qa.q: What happened when Mr Bhatia raised his voice?
qa.a: His request went on the board in red.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling in those meetings?
qa.a: He was probably anxious to avoid conflict and exhausted, pulled by whoever pushed hardest.

qa.q: What could Sahil try instead in planning meetings?
qa.a: He could agree shared goals and a scoring method before the meeting, so quiet teams' requests are weighed on facts, not volume.

qa.q: How might the call centre staff see the planning meetings?
qa.a: They feel their input doesn't matter, which is why they stopped attending while complaints piled up.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching a manager give in to the most forceful voices, so quieter teams feel ignored and the product drifts.
